title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
formal:
Determine the function
\[F(W,\lambda)=\sup_{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(W)}\bigl(\lambda R_{1}+(1-\lambda)R_{2}\bigr)\]
for every finite discrete memoryless broadcast channel \(W\) with a rational transition table and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]\). Here \(C(W)\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, deterministic codes, vanishing joint average decoding error, and no feedback, as defined below. The required accuracy is absolute \(1/100\) bit per channel use throughout this entire domain.
definitions:
For a positive integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{0,\ldots,m-1\}\). The domain contains all positive integers \(a,b,c\), alphabets \(\mathcal X=[a]\), \(\mathcal Y=[b]\), \(\mathcal Z=[c]\), and arrays \(W(y,z\mid x)\in\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) such that \(\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y,z\in\mathcal Z}W(y,z\mid x)=1\) for every \(x\). Alphabet sizes are unbounded, and zero transition probabilities are allowed. There is no conditional-independence requirement on the two outputs in a single use. For each block length \(n\ge1\), the channel law is
\[\Pr(Y^{n}=y^{n},Z^{n}=z^{n}\mid X^{n}=x^{n})=\prod_{t=1}^{n}W(y_{t},z_{t}\mid x_{t}).\]
The table specifies the whole channel; it has no additional state or memory.

An \((n,K_{1},K_{2})\) code, with positive integer message sizes, consists of maps \(f:[K_{1}]\times[K_{2}]\to\mathcal X^{n}\), \(d_{1}:\mathcal Y^{n}\to[K_{1}]\), and \(d_{2}:\mathcal Z^{n}\to[K_{2}]\). The messages \(M_{1},M_{2}\) are independent and uniform, the encoder transmits \(f(M_{1},M_{2})\), and the receivers output \(d_{1}(Y^{n})\) and \(d_{2}(Z^{n})\). Its joint average error is
\[P_{e}=\Pr\bigl[d_{1}(Y^{n})\ne M_{1}\ \text{or}\ d_{2}(Z^{n})\ne M_{2}\bigr],\]
where the probability averages over both messages and the specified channel randomness. No worst-case-over-messages error requirement is imposed. The encoder knows both messages; each decoder observes only its own output block. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, shared randomness, secrecy condition, or input-cost constraint. Codes are arbitrary deterministic maps with no uniform construction or complexity bound. Dependence among the transmitted symbols and deterministic time sharing are allowed.

All logarithms defining rates have base two; rates and the target function are measured in bits per channel use. A pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{2}\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes, indexed by \(j\ge1\), with \(n_{j}\to\infty\), \(P_{e,j}\to0\), and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}\log_{2}(K_{i,j})/n_{j}\ge R_{i}\) for both \(i=1,2\). Define \(C(W)\) as the Euclidean closure of the achievable pairs. It is a nonempty compact convex downward-closed subset of \([0,\log_{2}b]\times[0,\log_{2}c]\); these properties and the endpoint weights make \(F\) a finite real function, including when an alphabet has size one. A supremum in the definition does not require a finite code attaining a boundary rate. Its exact values at all rational weights determine the closed region; the benchmark below requires only their stated approximation.

If an answer is given as an algorithm, its finite input is the three alphabet sizes followed by the full table in lexicographic order and the weight, with integers in binary and rational numbers as reduced numerator/positive-denominator pairs separated by delimiters. All valid inputs in this encoding are included. No time bound or fixed grammar for a mathematical answer is imposed.
answer_criterion:
Supply one unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the entire domain above and a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[\forall W\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1],\qquad |g(W,\lambda)-F(W,\lambda)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The proof must match the code model, average error, limiting convention, units, and unbounded range of alphabet sizes. It must justify both sides of the error guarantee against the operational capacity definition. Certified bounds \(L(W,\lambda)\le F(W,\lambda)\le U(W,\lambda)\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualify through their midpoint. An exact determination also qualifies. Any submitted evaluation algorithm must terminate for every valid input and certify its returned value; a mathematical expression is not required to have a prescribed computational complexity. Sampled agreement, an uncertified numerical optimizer, a one-sided achievable or converse bound, and a renaming of the defining supremum or an unevaluated limiting characterization do not suffice. Resolving whether one particular inner bound is exact is not by itself the requested function, and an impossibility result for a different evaluation task does not replace this answer.
why: One of the smallest communication networks whose full capacity region is unknown. It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

importance.reason: A central multiuser capacity problem with a precisely defined rate region, decades of partial characterizations and recent challenges to the longstanding candidate inner bound.

progress.text: Marton gives a general achievable region for independent private messages and identifies special capacity cases.

The checked v3 of Gohari–Anantharam gives auxiliary-cardinality bounds, closedness and computability of the inner region, and a mismatch with a known outer region; the journal publication followed in 2012.
Geng and coauthors obtain capacity for new product-channel classes and show that the UV outer bound can be loose.
Dou and coauthors publish numerical bound-evaluation algorithms with convergence guarantees under specified concavity and initialization conditions.
The checked Gohari–Liu–Nair full manuscript gives stronger outer bounds and example improvements; it still describes general capacity as unknown.

Huang–Liu–Liu v1 claims a finite unconstrained counterexample to full one-letter Marton optimality, including an explicit rational enlarged channel. This narrower claim is not an independently verified capacity solution.

status_note: Individually checked on 14 September 2026. The checked primary literature, including the January 2026 outer-bound manuscript and Huang–Liu–Liu’s 20 August 2026 v1, describes the general exact capacity characterization as open. The latter claims only strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton inner bound, with an explicit rational enlarged channel, and would not supply the requested capacity function even if correct. Its proof and numerical certificates have not been independently verified. The 2024 numerical convergence results have explicit hypotheses and concern bounds. Bounded later-work and rational-channel evaluation searches found no matching full solution; historical exact-question openness does not independently certify the fixed 1/100 benchmark as unsolved. Retained as source_open with these limits.

context_blocks.text: One transmitter must convey two independent messages through a single stream of inputs. Each receiver sees its own noisy observations, so the possible pairs of reliable rates form a tradeoff region. Unlike an interference channel, there are no separately informed transmitters. This is a central network information theory question because even the general two-receiver case lacks a known evaluable capacity characterization in the checked sources.

The two individual capacities do not determine the joint region. If the same noiseless input bit reaches both receivers, either receiver alone can receive one bit per use, but the private rates satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le1\). If the input is instead a pair of bits and each receiver receives its designated bit, the region is \([0,1]^{2}\), although both individual capacities are still one. These examples distinguish the shared resource in the question from two independent point-to-point capacity calculations.

Marton’s 1979 region is a general achievable inner bound, and the original paper identifies channel classes for which capacity is known. Its two independent private messages match this card. The original separate average-error requirements and this card’s vanishing probability that either decoder fails are equivalent by elementary probability bounds; neither is the maximal-message error criterion.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite bounds on the auxiliary alphabet sizes in Marton’s inner region, making that region closed and computable. Their formulation permits a common message; setting its rate to zero gives the private-message slice relevant here. They also establish that this inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region can differ. This gap alone does not identify which bound is loose, and computability of an inner region does not establish its equality with capacity.

Geng and coauthors determine capacity for certain product-channel classes and prove that the UV outer bound is not always tight. Their full version also explains the multiletter sum-rate characterization: normalized Marton sum rates on successively longer repeated channels recover the operational sum capacity in the limit. This limiting equality supplies no general finite stopping guarantee for the numerical answer requested here. Nonadditivity of Marton’s inner bound must not be confused with a failure of the usual rate normalization for repeated uses of the channel itself.

Dou and coauthors give numerical methods for evaluating several inner and outer bounds. Their Theorems 5–7 prove convergence under explicit hypotheses: the initial distribution and a global maximizer must lie in a suitable connected superlevel set, and the objective must be concave there. These are conditional convergence results, not an unconditional global capacity evaluator. Even exact optimization of a bound would still leave the issue of its tightness. Their numerical conventions use natural logarithms unless otherwise specified; this card fixes bits throughout.

Gohari, Liu and Nair’s 2026 manuscript strengthens sum-rate outer bounds through two auxiliary receivers, with a full-region version in its appendix and numerical improvements for skew-symmetric examples. The auxiliary receivers are proof variables, not extra terminals available to a code. The reported improvements still leave inner/outer gaps and do not give the general function.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s preprint of 20 August 2026 claims strict suboptimality of the complete one-letter Marton region. A fixed-input-distribution example has ternary input; their separate constraint-removal theorem and explicit construction produce an unconstrained channel on a much larger finite alphabet. Section III.D specifies rational mixing probabilities and a rational joint channel, so that example is within this card’s domain. It should not be described as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample. The claim concerns a gap from an inner bound, not a matching capacity evaluation. Its full proof and interval-arithmetic certificates were not independently verified or rerun in this review.

The rational-table domain is the saved editorial specialization of the general capacity question. The absolute \(1/100\) acceptance rule follows the user-approved numerical formulation of 12 September 2026 and is retained here. It is not an assertion of exact equality with any proposed capacity curve. The checked literature discusses the underlying exact characterization; this review does not infer that a historical open-status statement alone proves that the fixed-tolerance benchmark remains unsolved.

sentences: One transmitter sends two independent private messages through a memoryless channel to receivers with different noisy observations.
The target is the weighted support function of the average-error capacity region for every finite rational channel table and rational weight between zero and one.
All rates are measured in bits per channel use, and the two individual capacities do not determine the joint tradeoff.
Classical and recent work provides achievable regions, converse bounds and special cases, while the August 2026 Marton-suboptimality preprint is a narrower unverified claim.
A complete Lean proof must certify a supplied function within absolute error 1/100 over the entire stated domain.
